Senator Mark Kelly (D-AZ) introduced the Make AI Work for Americans Act, landmark legislation designed to make sure companies benefiting the most from AI pay their fair share and invest in American workers. The bill establishes a dedicated federal trust fund to support American workers, job seekers, and communities as the economy changes. Since its introduction, the bill has received broad support from national leaders.

See what supporters of the Make AI Work for Americans Act are saying here:

“It’s critical that legislators in Washington and in state capitols around the country begin to act now to help Americans make a successful transition to an AI economy. We can’t leave workers behind — as we have in the past — if we want to win the global AI competition. I applaud Senator Kelly for his leadership on this issue in Congress and for his legislation to make sure that AI works for working people,” said Gina Raimondo, CEO, RAISE US, former U.S. Secretary of Commerce.

“Senator Mark Kelly has introduced legislation that says the companies profiting from artificial intelligence have an obligation to the workers that technology displaces. His bill puts real money behind job training, behind paid work that carries a credential, and behind a stronger safety net for people who lose employment through no fault of their own,” said Reverend Al Sharpton, President, National Action Network.

Click here to read NAN’s full letter of support.

“At a time when many are urging our policymakers to take AI’s potential disruption seriously, it is good to see in this legislation a set of policies aimed at mitigating AI’s negative impacts on workers—from those just starting out to those displaced mid-career,” said Erika McEntarfer, former Commissioner of the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS).

“The early part of my career was building Internet platforms and I watched policy arrive years after the consequences did. We cannot repeat that same mistake in the AI era. Senator Kelly’s bill strengthens protections for workers before the disruption hits. And it is paid for by the industry, so the cost doesn’t fall on workers alone,” said Jason Goldman, technologist and former White House Chief Digital Officer.

“The public is looking for Congress to step up quickly to make sure AI development and deployment benefits workers, not just wealthy investors and executives. Senator Kelly’s bill offers many good ideas to push AI adoption in a pro-worker direction,” said Bharat Ramamurti, former Deputy Director of the White House National Economic Council.

“Senator Kelly’s Make AI Work for Americans Act represents a major step forward in rejecting an AI future that concentrates gains for the few while leaving millions of hard-working Americans behind. The Act provides admirably detailed revenue proposals to ensure that those profiting from AI-induced displacement of workers, help fund a major increase in opportunities for workers to transition to new careers, start new businesses, attain National Service jobs while also ensuring that unemployment benefits are substantial enough to support a worker’s family while they strive to attain these new jobs. Importantly, Senator Kelly’s call for a major expansion of National Service jobs could provide entry level workers being squeezed out by AI the chance to both serve their country and gain valuable work experience, judgment and managerial skills,” said Gene Sperling, Director of the National Economic Council for Presidents Clinton and Obama, Senior Advisor to President Biden, Director of the Economic Dignity Lab at McCourt School at Georgetown.

Gene Sperling on X: Kudos to @SenMarkKelly for not waiting for major AI job dislocation to start laying the foundation for putting jobs & workers first. His bill admirably lays out specific AI revenue sources to fund not only needed training, but also National Service jobs & entrepreneurship.

“Senator Kelly has been thoughtfully wrestling with the concerns that real Americans are facing with the adoption of AI — job displacement, costs, and ensuring that the benefits of this technology don’t just accrue to the few. This keeps the focus on ensuring Americans win,” said Mieke Eoyang, former Deputy Assistant Secretary of Defense for Cyber Policy.

“The companies that are ushering in AI should pay to fix the societal harms it will cause. Senator Kelly’s legislation is built on that idea. This bill puts industry dollars into supporting workers whose jobs are changing and gives everyone the resources to adapt. It will take effort from private companies and government leadership to make sure this technology develops responsibly, and I believe this bill is the right way to start,” said Jon A. Shirley, former President, Chief Operating Officer, and Director of Microsoft.

“A safe AI future and a fair AI economy are two sides of the same promise. With one in five American workers expected to be Latino by 2030, our community has an enormous stake in seeing that promise kept. Senator Kelly’s Make AI Work for Americans Act ensures that as the AI industry grows, so do our investments in the workers who power the American economy. This legislation invests in paid service-to-career pathways, community college and apprenticeship programs, and capital for new small businesses. It gives workers who lose their jobs real stability as they retrain and find their next opportunity; and it helps close the digital divide by supporting digital access for participants, building AI literacy into our workforce system, and making resources available to people with limited English proficiency. It also gives workers and civil rights organizations a seat at the table as AI enters the workplace. This legislation lays the foundation for modernizing how we support workers and workplaces in the age of AI. UnidosUS is proud to endorse it and urges Congress to pass it,” said Eric Rodriguez, Senior Vice President of Policy & Advocacy, UnidosUS.

“Artificial intelligence is rapidly changing the nature of work, and our workforce development systems must evolve alongside it. JFF is proud to support the Make AI Work for Americans Act, which invests in the systems already serving workers while expanding access to education and training, strengthening service-to-career pathways, supporting entrepreneurship, and helping workers navigate technological change. We applaud Senator Kelly’s leadership in advancing a vision for AI that puts workers at the center and helps ensure technological progress creates greater economic opportunity for people and communities across the country,” said Maria Flynn, President and CEO, Jobs for the Future (JFF).

“The greatest barrier to older Americans participating in the AI economy is not their willingness to learn, but access to opportunities. Older Americans are ready to embrace AI and develop the skills needed to succeed in a changing workplace. What they need is access to training and investments in their potential. Our economy cannot afford to overlook this extraordinary source of talent,” said Gary. A. Officer, Founder & CEO, CWI Labs.

“Senator Kelly’s Make AI Work for Americans Act is a series of policy proposals focused on what Americans will need most in the AI age. If AI has the transformative impact on our society that those who are building it say it will, we will need new ideas and a safety net for our workforce, small businesses, and more. This bill focuses on how to deliver real benefits to Americans impacted by AI and makes sure companies pay their fair share to ensure that AI works for all of us. It’s refreshing to see real leaders rising to the challenge of the AI age and we applaud the Senator for his efforts,” said Neera Tanden, President and CEO of the Center for American Progress.

“As artificial intelligence transforms our classrooms and communities, we have a generational responsibility to ensure that every student and worker is equipped to navigate this new landscape. The Make AI Work for Americans Act takes a vital, inclusive approach, anchored by robust investments in education, AI literacy, and workforce alignment, so that all Americans can share in the remarkable opportunities of artificial intelligence while safeguarding against its risks,” said Erin Mote, CEO, InnovateEDU.

“It is important that Congress recognizes that we need a greater investment in worker transitions, particularly given the possibility for a dramatic reshaping of our economy due to rapid advancement in technology. Senator Kelly and his staff have done a great job thinking about the most pressing issues with unemployment insurance, especially right now. I hope this legislation gets the serious consideration that it deserves,” said Michele Evermore, Senior Fellow for Worker Transitions, National Employment Law Project.

“This act would empower underserved communities with the necessary tools to help shape their lives and our collective future via system innovation, especially for small businesses. At the same time, it addresses the existing digital divide by opening new pathways to unexplored economic opportunity, competition, and equity. It turns AI into a participatory device accessible to all, rather than a passive application intended for and controlled by a few,” said Robert Alvarado, Senior Vice President, Chicanos Por La Causa.

“AmeriCorps and the nation’s state service commissions connect service to careers, provide hands-on experience, skill development, and pathways to meaningful work. We applaud Senator Kelly’s leadership in introducing the Make AI Work for Americans Act and his recognition of the National Service for America’s Future program to expand paid service opportunities that lead to credentials, careers, and durable skills. As technology reshapes the workplace, national service can play an important role in preparing workers and strengthening communities. State service commissions stand ready to help turn this vision into opportunities that meet local workforce needs across the country,” said John Kelly, CEO, America’s Service Commissions.

“Artificial intelligence is rapidly reshaping the labor market, including many of the entry-level jobs that have traditionally helped young people get a foothold in the workforce. The Make AI Work for Americans Act recognizes that national service should be part of the solution. By building on AmeriCorps as a backbone for new service-to-career opportunities and exploring ways to strengthen AmeriCorps, this legislation would help more Americans build durable skills, gain meaningful work experience, and pursue credentials and careers while meeting critical needs in their communities. We thank Senator Kelly for recognizing national service as an important part of the workforce infrastructure our country will need as AI transforms the economy,” said AnnMaura Connolly, President, Voices for National Service.

“As Congress writes the rules for what comes next, young people must be at the center of it. They’re entering a job market where the entry-level roles that used to launch careers are changing fast. Americans across the ideological spectrum support national service, and states are equipped to scale it. Every time this country has faced a shift this large, it has answered with service, from the Civilian Conservation Corps in the Depression to the GI Bill after World War II. Today’s challenge deserves an answer of the same ambition. Senator Kelly is putting one on the table, and we are grateful for his leadership,” said Vicky Hausman, Founder & CEO, American Service Project.

Click here to read the full text of the bill, here for a section-by-section, and here for a one-pager.

matches.text:
ICYMI: At HELP Hearing, Murray Grills Trump Nominees on AI Denying Seniors’ Health Care

ICYMI: On Senate Floor, Murray Urges Colleagues to End Trump Administration’s AI Program that is Delaying and Denying Seniors’ Health Care

***VIDEO OF FULL ROUNDTABLE DISCUSSION HERE***

***PHOTOS HERE***

Vancouver, WA — Today, U.S. Senators Patty Murray (D-WA), Vice Chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee and former chair of the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions (HELP) Committee, and Ron Wyden (D-OR), ranking member of the Senate Committee on Finance, held a roundtable discussion with providers to discuss how the Wasteful and Inappropriate Service Reduction (WISeR) model, a new pilot program implemented by the Trump administration that’s using artificial intelligence (AI) to conduct prior authorization in Traditional Medicare, has been overruling doctors and denying or delaying critical health care for seniors. The WISeR pilot model began on January 1, 2026, and is set to last for six years in six selected states, including Washington state.

Joining Senators Murray and Wyden for the discussion at the Area Agency on Aging & Disabilities of Southwest Washington today were: Dr. Keren Rosenblum, MD, MBA, President, The Vancouver Clinic; Dr. Leon McCook, family medicine physician, PeaceHealth; and Dr. Ettore Palazzo, MD, FACP, CEO, EvergreenHealth.

“Despite a lot of empty promises from Republicans to not cut Medicare—Trump’s new WISeR model is essentially a cut to Medicare. What else do you call it when seniors are getting cut off from the health care they need, for no good reason? Under this dystopian system—Washington state seniors are seeking doctor-recommended care to treat debilitating pain, only to be told by Trump’s AI system that Medicare won’t pay for it, or that they must wait weeks on end to get their treatment,” said Senator Murray. “The truth is—the WISeR model has been a complete mess. This cannot continue—and it absolutely cannot expand. That’s why I’m here to continue talking with folks on the ground—patients, doctors and more—and gathering evidence and stories we can use to make the case back in Congress. We are going to keep pushing hard to stop private companies from raiding Medicare, and cheating seniors with AI. Republicans may be sitting on their hands but a Democratic majority will be aggressive in pushing back and working to end this experiment, and save Medicare.”

“Dr. Frankenstein isn’t the only one conducting dangerous experiments this Halloween season. The mad scientists given free rein in the Trump administration are quite willing to risk seniors’ access to lifesaving health care with their latest scheme grafting AI on to authorization decisions for traditional Medicare,” said Senator Wyden. “As the ranking member of the Senate Finance Committee overseeing Medicare, I’m proud to stand with Senator Murray in the battle against Trump empowering unaccountable AI companies to delay and deny certain types of care in traditional Medicare.”

“Physicians support innovation and efforts to reduce waste and improve value in health care. But those goals should not come at the expense of timely access to medically necessary care,” said Dr. Keren Rosenblum, MD, MBA, President, The Vancouver Clinic. “WISeR moves Traditional Medicare toward the same prior authorization system physicians already know creates administrative burdens, delays appropriate care, and creates uncertainty for patients. At a time when physicians are already facing significant administrative burdens and workforce challenges, we should be looking for ways to make health care simpler—not adding new layers of complexity. Innovation should strengthen the patient-physician relationship, not create new obstacles between patients and the care their physicians believe they need.”

“After almost a full year of WISeR, it is clear how its implementation has negatively impacted our patients and staff, but we are still unsure if the program is achieving its intended purpose. As a community-owned public hospital district, EvergreenHealth supports efforts to reduce fraud, waste and the inappropriate utilization of Medicare benefits. However, we must pursue those goals in a way that does not delay care nor create unnecessary hardship for the patients we serve,” saidDr. Ettore Palazzo, MD, FACP, CEO, EvergreenHealth. “In the months following WISeR’s January implementation, we saw patients live with prolonged pain due to delayed authorizations for their treatment. Confusion and inconsistent processes have created additional workloads for our providers, making it difficult for them to support their patients effectively. Let’s continue to improve quality, value and program integrity in Medicare, but let’s focus on patient-centered implementation, timely decision-making and reducing unnecessary burdens on our care teams.”

Under the WISeR model, patients on Traditional Medicare across six states—Arizona, New Jersey, Oklahoma, Ohio, Texas, and Washington—are subject to prior authorization requirements for several types of procedures or treatments, meaning that a claim needs to run through an opaque A.I.-driven system that may deny it with limited explanation. This forces starting the whole approval process over again and setting the patient back weeks in the process. Several of the procedures subject to prior authorization under the WISeR model are treatments for patients experiencing debilitating pain, who are now having to wait to receive necessary care. Before this model, patients would have been able to receive care within the same week, or even day, in most cases. Prior authorization requirements are used routinely by Medicare Advantage plans and private insurers, but rarely in Traditional Medicare—which is often one of the reasons seniors choose it for their coverage. While the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) has described the model as voluntary, it is effectively mandatory for providers and their patients with Traditional Medicare in the selected states.

Each participating state is operating the pilot through a different for-profit company that contracts with CMS to use AI technology to process prior authorizations and conduct reviews for the specific services subject to WISeR. These participants are compensated based on a share of “averted expenditures.” In other words, they are financially incentivized to deny prior authorization requests, as they profit from denied services.

Senators Murray and Wyden have been pushing back on this harmful pilot program from the start, and for the past year and a half, Murray has been meeting with providers and patients across the state to hear about the implementation and harms of this program. In September of last year, Senators Murray, Wyden and other Senate Democrats sent a letter to CMS Administrator Dr. Mehmet Oz and Center for Medicare and Medicaid Innovation (CMMI) Director Abe Sutton, urging CMS to halt implementation of the model until a full analysis is conducted of the program’s impact on patient access—which, they argued, should include input from beneficiaries and their families, consumer and patient advocates, health care providers and suppliers. In December last year, Senators Murray and Wyden introduced the Seniors Deserve SMARTER (Streamlined Medical Approvals for Timely, Efficient Recovery) Care Act, legislation that would prohibit CMS from implementing the WISeR model that began on January 1, 2026.

This July, Murray and Wyden forced a vote on a Congressional Review Act (CRA) resolution to overturn the WISeR program—Republicans chose to side with the Trump administration and blocked the CRA. In September, Senator Murray grilled Chris Klomp, the nominee to be Deputy Secretary of Health and Human Services (HHS), on the WISeR model and how the private companies conducting the prior authorization assessments are profiting from the denials.

Senator Murray is also an original cosponsor of the bipartisan Improving Seniors’ Timely Access to Care Act of 2025 to streamline and crack down on prior authorization practices in Medicare Advantage plans.

###

matches.text:
PROVIDENCE, RI -- As major retailers begin using artificial intelligence (AI) to make so-called ‘surveillance pricing’ or ‘personal pricing’ more intrusive, unfair, and opaque, U.S. Senator Jack Reed is seeking to prevent companies from unfairly charging consumers more based on personal data algorithms.

Personalized or individualized price discrimination broadly refers to the practice of retailers “using troves of personal data to set individualized prices. As a result, people are paying different amounts for the same exact product, just because businesses are better equipped to infer who will pay more.”

During a visit to the Bom Café in Providence today, Senator Reed joined café owner Rosie Santana and Nina Harrison, Policy Director of the Economic Progress Institute (EPI), for a conversation about the importance of marketplace fairness and preventing unfair AI-enabled cost manipulation.

“Consumers deserve transparent pricing and equal treatment, not hidden technology that misuses their personal data to set different prices for the same item and charge some shoppers more than others. AI is a powerful tool, but it presents real and pressing challenges. This is one of them and Congress needs to take thoughtful, concrete steps to ban exploitative AI-enabled price discrimination and ensure fairness in the marketplace. Whether it’s food, coffee, or basic staples, no family should pay hidden premiums and higher prices for the same product based on their personal online data that has been collected without their knowledge or consent,” said Senator Reed.

The Economic Progress Institute recently released its biennial Rhode Island Standard of Need report offering a snapshot of what it costs for individuals and families to afford a no-frills life in Rhode Island. The 2026 report calculates monthly and annual budgets for housing, food, transportation, health care, child care, and other essentials—and shows that nearly 40 percent of Rhode Island households may not have enough income to meet their basic needs.

“Rhode Islanders literally cannot afford to have surveillance pricing in this state. They cannot afford for companies to take their personal information and use that personal information against them to raise prices and make things even less affordable. Working families can’t afford it. We can't allow it. And that’s why I’m so grateful to Senator Reed for doing this work and raising this issue to try to get ahead of it and prevent surveillance pricing before it harms Rhode Islanders,” said EPI’s Policy Director Nina Harrison.

An investigation by Consumer Reports and Groundwork Collaborative found that popular grocery apps like Instacart used AI-enabled pricing experiments to inflate the grocery bills of some users. AI-powered algorithms led to some shoppers getting charged $3.99 for a box of Wheat Thins, while another shopper from the same store at the same time was charged $4.89. Based on how much Instacart estimates a typical household of four spends on groceries, the average price variations observed could translate into a cost swing of $1,200 per year on food alone.

Senator Reed says there should be federal guardrails and clear, durable consumer protection laws in place that keep pace with the needs of Americans and rapidly-evolving technology.

Businesses have long used algorithmic pricing to determine how much consumers are willing to pay for products and services. But those systems set general prices for the masses based on supply, demand, competitor prices, and other broad data points. These new exploitative AI-enabled algorithms use personal data as a tool for price discrimination to try to ensure every consumer pays the maximum.

As AI becomes more common-place, more companies are starting to experiment with ‘personalized’ or ‘surveillance’ pricing, including the use of personal information such as browsing history, demographics, or behavioral patterns, and companies typically collect and analyze the data using AI and algorithms to charge different prices for different customers, based on a range of factors, such as their income, zip code/geolocation, mouse movements, or other personal data.

Reed is urging Congress to take bipartisan action to crack down on algorithmic price discrimination and prevent companies from using non-public data and artificial intelligence to unfairly squeeze every last penny out of consumers.

“If federal lawmakers fail to act, online shoppers will be at increased risk of price gouging, cost manipulation, and data privacy threats as more businesses use AI to target the finances, privacy, and equality of consumers,” said Senator Reed. “To ensure a healthy and prosperous Rhode Island, we must ensure working families can afford basic necessities. I will work across the aisle to ban AI-enabled price discrimination while ensuring companies can continue offering targeted discounts, promotions, rewards, loyalty and membership benefits, or contextual pricing.”

Many consumers are already being charged more money through ‘dynamic pricing’ for things like rideshares, airline tickets, and hotels whose prices can go up when demand is high and change based on timing and location. But even dynamic pricing is a concept that raises prices for all consumers, not just certain individuals.

matches.text:
San Francisco, CA — This week, U.S. Senator Adam Schiff (D-Calif.) discussed his view on rapidly developing AI capabilities and the role of Congress in regulating the technology during an interview with Punchbowl News co-founders Jake Sherman and Anna Palmer at the publication’s first-ever Tech Summit in San Francisco.

In the wide-ranging discussion, Schiffhighlighted his legislation to ensure private industry pays for the energy they use amid the buildout of data centers – so that Americans are not forced to pay higher energy costs as a result of the AI boom – and discussed Democrats’ approach to AI oversight next year, noting that Americans should “expect constructive oversight, not destructive oversight.”

Schiff also discussedthe risks he sees in rapidly advancing AI models and argued that concerns about competition with China should include prioritization of safety, developing a skilled workforce, and improving education.

View the full interview here.

Key Excerpts:

On Democrats’ AI priorities should control of Congress flip:

[…] I think the industry should expect constructive oversight, not destructive oversight. I think it should expect a Democratic majority that wants technology to succeed, wants these jobs to stay in America, wants their contribution to the economy and medicine and science but believes in regulation. Does not believe that any group of people be by dint of their wealth are empowered to make decisions affecting all of society for themselves. I think that’s what they should expect.

[…] What I do want to see is oversight that leads to sensible regulation of an industry that can do a lot of good and can do a lot of harm. To minimize the harms, to protect against the harms, do what government is supposed to do. I want to see a Congress that does what we have done in the past when we also had massive powerful corporations but we’re not afraid to regulate them. That is a basic function of government.

On why Congress must move quickly to put guardrails on advanced AI:

[…] I do think we need to put in place protocols and monitors, a system to make sure that as these frontier models are developing, they’re developing safely. That there are processes in place where we don’t have to simply take the word of the companies that ‘don’t worry we’re doing it safely.’ I certainly don’t believe the self-policing; the moral authority argument is sufficient. There’s just too much profit motive, too much of a collective action problem that confronts the whole industry globally.

[…] You train the power of AI to find out everything it can about a single individual. Do we really think that their health records or their purchases or their subscriptions or any of their data is beyond the reach of an AI agent, sophisticated model, trying to find out the personal information? And with all the Flock cameras and with all the other CCTV cameras and the vulnerability of those systems, are we going to have any privacy left? And I think unless Congress acts, there won’t be any privacy left.

On ensuring AI development is safe as we compete with China to establish AI dominance:

[…] I get that we should be very concerned about China’s advances in this area. I don’t want to dismiss that argument. That’s an argument that says that we need to reach some kind of an accord with China, which won’t be easy to do, but we need to do our best. It is not an argument though that, because China is making advances and we want to stay ahead of China, that we should rush headlong with the development of these models and regenerative AI in such a way that well, ‘let’s be sure that if we kill ourselves we do it first rather than letting China do it.’ We still want to make sure what we’re doing is safe for our people and safe for others.

[…] Why don’t we focus on improving our education system? Improving STEM education, making sure that everyone who graduates from high school has a good solid education, that the doors of higher education are open. Let’s compete with China on a skilled workforce. Let’s compete with China in how we think about the integration and the manufacturing of products that will incorporate AI. That’s where a lot of the economic benefits are going to come.

On passing legislation to protect Americans from absorbing higher costs from data center buildouts:

[…] I introduced an early bill on this that would insist essentially that these data centers pay their own way. That they not only develop their own energy, but also that they have additional capacity to put energy into the grid during peak times. That they are responsible for the upgrades to the regional system that those costs are not socialized to others. It’s not hard to require that. It’s certainly not going to be done just by some kind of, ‘well, we give you our word.’

[…] There should be complete transparency. I don’t think people should be misled about a project and then suddenly learn it’s going to be a data center in their backyard. But I don’t think everywhere is the same and I think communities should make the decision. Do they want it? Do they not want it? And some communities may want it, and many will not want it and that ought to be a decision that is made locally and I think not nationally. But we should be insistent nationally that those costs and burdens not be socialized onto others.

On the Senate’s latest proposal for permitting reform:

[…] We absolutely need permitting reform, and it looks like we may be close. What I’m going to be particularly looking at, and the text was just released, so we’re all kind of digging through it, is this going to be just regulatory reform for the oil and gas industry? Is this really just going to be used to advance those two sources of energy or, is this going to be advantageous to renewables? And what about in an administration in which there is almost a theocratic objection to anything but oil and gas? We’ve seen our state punished repeatedly by this president who only represents those states that he won. Is that going to continue? Are there any meaningful limits on that in this permitting reform? That’s what I’m going to be looking at.

###

matches.text:
Schiff on the need for bipartisan action on AI regulation: “Increasingly, as people hear from their constituents, there’ll be bipartisan interest in legislating this area.”

Washington, D.C. – This week, U.S. Senator Adam Schiff (D-Calif.) detailed his AI priorities during an appearance on The Verge’s Decoder Podcast with Nilay Patel. During the interview, Schiff highlighted the need for enforceable industry-wide guardrails that protect against the potential harms of frontier AI development and underscored that voluntary commitments like the framework put forward by Donald Trump would not be enough.

Schiff also noted that if control of Congress changes, Democrats will pursue oversight of harmful AI incidents, noting: “You’re going to see vigorous oversight in this area… We’re going to want the leaders of this industry to come in and talk about all of the times that their own agents have gotten away from them, how it happened, what’s been done about it, and what they’re doing about it. We’re going to want these companies to be transparent with Congress about it.”

The Senator also voiced support for the establishment of a regulatory body designed with the high expertise and discretion necessary to keep up with advanced model development.

View the full interview here.

Key Excerpts:

On how Congress’s failure to regulate social media should inform its approach to putting guardrails on AI:

I’ll be honest, very circumspect about Congress and legislating the tech sector because we did such a — I don’t know what language I’m allowed to use here — but such a shitty job when it comes to any kind of regulation of the harms, the societal harms coming out of social media. We’re going to have to do a much better job and much more quickly when it comes to AI, because the threats are even more significant and we’re already at the point of strong potential harms. It can’t wait. We certainly can’t take the kind of years we’ve taken to try to even wrap ourselves around social media.

On how Democrats would conduct tech industry oversight if control of Congress flips:

You’re going to see vigorous oversight in this area to begin with. We’re going to want the leaders of this industry to come in and talk about all of the times that their own agents have gotten away from them, how it happened, what’s been done about it, and what they’re doing about it. We’re going to want these companies to be transparent with Congress about it. We’re going to want to legislate in this area, and that may come into conflict with the president, but there’s a lot of bipartisan work product here. And I think that given where the country is and where it’s moving, it becomes increasingly difficult for this president to veto bipartisan work product coming out of the Congress. So that is my hope. It’s certainly a far better prospect than we have today. This is going to be a very central priority for the American people. We want to harness AI for the good it can do. We want to use it to bring down the cost of things. That’s our central priority. And there are ways that AI might be useful in bringing down certain costs. We want to protect the dignity of work also, but we want to make sure that this doesn’t pose a threat to the American people.

On Trump’s voluntary AI regulatory framework not being enough to match the threat of frontier advancements:

It was interesting to see all those tech leaders there signing onto this voluntary pledge on the one hand and on the other hand, away from the White House grounds, away from the president, being very public and saying, “We need regulation. We don’t want this to be just ‘Trust us, we’ll do the right thing.’” So yeah, it was very distant, very jarring. None of these companies want to incur the wrath of this very vengeful president. Apparently, they will say what he wants them to say in his presence. But the reality is, there is a real national security threat here. As these models become more and more advanced, as they advance themselves through this recursive AI, we have less and less of a sense of what they’re doing, how they’re deciding what they’re deciding, and what they’re trying to access lawfully or unlawfully. That is a national security concern of the highest order. There are other security concerns too.

On the need for a regulatory body to keep up with advanced model development:

This debate is going to keep evolving as AI evolves and at a speed that is really much faster than Congress has proven capable of legislating. I like to say that in the technology world, Moore’s law is increasing productivity, doubling it every 18 months, and with AI, maybe that’s quadrupling it every five months. The legislative calendar works more on a Murphy’s law timetable. And I think that disparity is even more pronounced in the area of AI. What I think that translates into is that we’re going to need a regulatory body that has real discretion and real expertise that can move a lot quicker than Congress can. Whether that looks like an FDA for artificial intelligence or some other agency, I think that’s ultimately going to be necessary. That agency’s going to have to have real power and teeth and real expertise. It’s going to be a challenge, as with these independent monitors: if there’s a government component there, how do we afford that? Because there’s so much talent, and that talent can draw much bigger salaries in the private sector. But I do think we’re going to need a regulatory body in addition to whatever the overarching statutory framework is.

On the need for enforceable industry-wide regulation of AI and data center build outs:

Data centers are the most tangible way for people to express their concerns about their neighborhood, but also about their job, about the technology, and about the uncertainty of it all. And I think the initial concern, and I still think it’s quite a dominant concern, is over the impact on jobs and the nature of work. But what has reached the fore more recently is concern about runaway AI and the danger it poses. What will the concern look like a month or two months from now? I don’t know, but I do think it’s not going away. And as the AI bills — and I’ve introduced several — indicate, not just mine, but others, most of those bills are bipartisan. […] My bill on the data centers would force them to pay the costs so that consumers don’t have to. It’s not the voluntary, “we pledge, we might, we’d like to; just don’t provide anything that will force us to observe those costs.” Those are mostly democratic bills. Republicans have largely adhered to the president’s line about not posing any real imposition. They want to pass fig-leaf kind of stuff, but not real stuff. But I think increasingly, as people hear from their constituents, there’ll be bipartisan interest in legislating this area.

###

Schumer Says Transformative 30-Year DOD Loan Commitment Positions Wolfspeed As A Supplier Of Silicon Carbide Semiconductors Essential To U.S. National Security, Catalyzing Domestic Chip Production & Creating Good-Paying Jobs In The Mohawk Valley

As Longtime Champion Of Wolfspeed, Schumer Previously Delivered The CHIPS Investment Tax Credit From His Bipartisan CHIPS & Science Law To Expand Production & Workforce At Wolfspeed’s Fab In Marcy

Schumer: We’re Making The Mohawk Valley A Key Stop On Upstate NY’s Rapidly Growing Semiconductor Superhighway

After leading a bipartisan delegation of U.S. Senators urging the Secretaries of Defense and Commerce to support a whole-of-government response to preserve and strengthen domestic manufacturing of silicon carbide, Schumer today announced a massive $1.5 billion investment from the U.S. Department of Defense (“DoD”) for Wolfspeed to supercharge manufacturing of its silicon carbide semiconductors, which are critical for next-generation applications across aerospace, defense, and infrastructure.

Schumer, building on years of tireless advocacy in support of Wolfspeed, including delivering the federal CHIPS Investment Tax Credit as part of his bipartisan CHIPS & Science Law, said that this 30-year, $1.5 billion loan commitment through the DoD’s Office of Strategic Capital would enable Wolfspeed to expand production of their state-of-the-art semiconductors for use by the defense supply chain, creating good-paying jobs at its industry-leading fab in the Mohawk Valley and would also expand Upstate New York’s rapidly growing Semiconductor Superhighway.

“I’ve been advocating for years for the federal investment needed for Wolfspeed to scale domestic production of silicon carbide chips, which this $1.5 billion DoD investment would supercharge. I have been leading the bipartisan charge to strengthen the domestic manufacturing of silicon carbide because of how critical it is to our national security and to outcompeting China. Wolfspeed is powering American technological leadership, national security, and international competitiveness from their state-of-the-art semiconductor fab at the Marcy Nanocenter, and their silicon carbide chips would define the next generation of innovation,” said Senator Schumer. “After fighting for more than a decade to transform Upstate New York into a globally recognized semiconductor superhighway, this is yet another example that the work is paying off here in Oneida County. I will never stop fighting to create good-paying jobs, protect our national security, and deliver for communities across the Mohawk Valley.”

In a recent bipartisan letter led by Schumer, he and the other senators explained that silicon carbide is the foundational substrate for a critical class of next-generation semiconductors thanks to its unique combination of high voltage tolerance, thermal conductivity, and switching speed, which make it both indispensable across advanced defense systems, electric grid infrastructure, 5G telecommunications, and the modern automotive sector.

“We believe the scale and 30-year tenor of this conditional commitment reflects the long-term importance of the technology and manufacturing capabilities Wolfspeed has built in the United States,” said Robert Feurle, Chief Executive Officer of Wolfspeed. “This financing would strengthen our continued advancement of silicon carbide materials and wide bandgap power devices, reinforcing our efforts to build a more resilient U.S. semiconductor and defense industrial base.”

On the heels of Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit to the U.S. and Beijing launching its Made in China 2025 initiative, making silicon carbide a national industrial, military, and economic priority, Schumer emphasized that accelerating U.S. global leadership in the development and production of cutting-edge silicon carbide, gallium nitride, and other high bandgap semiconductors produced by companies like Wolfspeed as well as onsemi, with operations in both the Hudson Valley and Central New York, is critical to countering China’s efforts to dominate the global silicon carbide semiconductor industry and supply chain. Over the last five years, Chinese producers have increased their share of the global silicon carbide market from under 5 percent to nearly 50 percent.

Schumer added, “As I’ve been warning for years, we cannot let the CCP get its hands on our advanced chips and the manufacturing equipment needed to produce them. It's time to stand up to Xi for the sake of the American people and for global security. We must act now to bolster and secure the silicon carbide semiconductor industry before it's too late.”

Schumer has fought for decades to position the Mohawk Valley and Upstate NY to attract billions of dollars in new investment, create tens of thousands of good-paying jobs, and ascend as a national leader in advanced manufacturing and defense technologies. In addition to creating the conditions for companies like Wolfspeed to grow and thrive, Schumer is actively working with Oneida County and Mohawk Valley EDGE to help lure additional semiconductor, manufacturing supply chain, and defense technology companies to the Marcy Nanocenter, which the Senator has long called one of the premier, shovel-ready sites in the entire country, as well as the Griffiss Business & Technology Park.

“This $1.5 billion federal commitment further demonstrates that the groundwork laid by Oneida County continues to pay off and recognizes the critical role Wolfspeed plays in the semiconductor ecosystem. The advanced semiconductor technologies being developed by Wolfspeed have important applications for our national defense and complement the groundbreaking research and innovation taking place at the Air Force Research Laboratory in Rome. Having these capabilities in our community strengthens Oneida County’s position in the nation’s semiconductor and defense technology ecosystem, and this announcement reinforces the importance of continuing to grow that presence. I thank Senator Schumer for his bipartisan work to help make this commitment possible and for his continued efforts to support semiconductor manufacturing and national security in our region,” said Anthony J. Picente Jr., Oneida County Executive

“Today’s announcement is another significant vote of confidence in Wolfspeed, the Marcy Nanocenter, and the growing semiconductor ecosystem taking root in Upstate New York. We are grateful to Senator Chuck Schumer for his relentless advocacy on behalf of Wolfspeed and the broader semiconductor industry. His leadership has helped position New York and the Mohawk Valley as critical contributors to America’s advanced manufacturing, economic competitiveness, and national security. This conditional financing commitment further reinforces the importance of Wolfspeed’s operations in Marcy and the long-term opportunities that lie ahead for our region,” said Marc Barraco, Chief of Staff, Mohawk Valley EDGE.

Thanks to Schumer’s bipartisan CHIPS & Science Law, Upstate New York is undergoing a historic transformation into an internationally recognized epicenter of semiconductor manufacturing, innovation, and workforce development. The senator landed and delivered billions of dollars to realize Micron’s historic $100+ billion semiconductor megafab in Onondaga County – which broke ground earlier this year and is currently proceeding ahead of schedule – creating over 50,000 new good-paying jobs and thousands of construction jobs. The senator fought for and successfully delivered a designation and $40 million implementation award to launch the NY Smart I-Corridor Tech Hub, establishing Upstate NY as a national hub for workforce training, innovation, and manufacturing of semiconductor technologies. The senator also delivered a $32 million CHIPS funding agreement for Corning Incorporated to fuel its $315 million investment to increase the production of its specialized glass vital for semiconductor manufacturing in Northern NY, creating 300 good-paying manufacturing and construction jobs.

Schumer has also been a leading champion for national security innovation and economic development across the region. Schumer has fought tirelessly to deliver billions of dollars in annual appropriations and federal contracts to Rome’s Air Force Research Lab, and drive hundreds of millions of dollars of annual economic impact across the Mohawk Valley and more than 1,000 good-paying jobs at Rome Lab and across its burgeoning defense industrial base. Schumer delivered a $30 million federal Defense Production Act investment, driving TTM Technologies’ $130 million expansion to manufacture cutting-edge printed circuit boards critical and create up to 400 good-paying jobs in the Town of DeWitt. Schumer has also successfully secured more than $100 million in annual appropriations and federal contracts over the last decade for Saab to expand the footprint of its global headquarters in East Syracuse, adding hundreds of good-paying new jobs and tens of thousands of square feet of new production capacity.

A copy of the Schumer-led delegation letterto the Secretary of Defense and Secretary of Commerce is included below:

Dear Secretaries Hegseth and Lutnick:

We write to draw your attention to a critical matter at the intersection of national security, economic competitiveness and trade policy: the accelerating Chinese government effort to dominate the global silicon carbide semiconductor industry and supply chain, and the urgent need for a whole-of-government response to preserve and strengthen trusted domestic and allied manufacturing of silicon carbide.

Silicon carbide is the foundational substrate for a critical class of next-generation semiconductors that are indispensable across advanced defense systems, AI data centers, electric grid infrastructure, 5G telecommunications, and the modern automotive sector. Silicon carbide's unique combination of high-voltage tolerance, thermal conductivity, and switching speed makes it irreplaceable in high-performance air, land and sea propulsion systems, directed energy weapons, and air and missile defense systems.

Since launching its Made in China 2025 initiative, Beijing has recognized the military and economic importance of silicon carbide and made global domination in the sector a national industrial priority. In the last five years, Chinese producers have increased their share of the global silicon carbide wafer market from less than 5 percent to nearly 50 percent today.

Clearly, China intends to undermine another strategically important industry built on American technology and ingenuity. If this campaign succeeds, the United States will find itself dependent on adversary supply chains for materials essential to our most advanced defense systems and critical technological infrastructure. The domestic supply chain is already under significant pressure and we are at risk of losing industry leaders and globally competitive manufacturers to this coordinated campaign. The time to act is now, before we reach the crisis stage where remedies are impossible or far more expensive and time-consuming.

We encourage you to leverage Defense Production Act authorities, critical minerals designations, Buy America requirements, and any other authorities at your disposal to ensure the U.S. can protect its silicon carbide supply chain.

###

matches.text:
Washington, D.C. – U.S. Senator Ron Wyden, D-Ore., called for the White House to release a report it commissioned examining the privacy impacts of surveillance activities funded by the Office of National Drug Control Policy (ONDCP), including a program that scoops up data from Flock cameras and other license plate readers across the country and a dragnet phone surveillance program called Hemisphere.

Wyden learned of the report as part of his oversight of the Hemisphere phone surveillance program, which mined trillions of American phone records under an arrangement between AT&T and the federal government. The White House ultimately ended that program in 2025 after repeated requests from Wyden and Rep. Andy Biggs, R-Ariz. The Hemisphere program was operated by the Houston High Intensity Drug Trafficking Area (HIDTA) program and paid for with funds from the ONDCP.

After Wyden began questioning ONDCP about its funding of the Hemisphere program, ONDCP informed Wyden’s staff that it had commissioned the nonprofit technology research firm MITRE to study privacy issues related to the HIDTA program. However, the ONDCP refused to share the report with Wyden’s office when it was finished in 2024, and has continued to keep it hidden from the public.

Recently, 404 Media reported that local law enforcement agencies are funneling data from Flock and other license plate reader cameras into a national database, also operated by the Houston HIDTA.

“Flock’s AI surveillance cameras have sparked a nationwide backlash against unnecessary government intrusion into Americans’ lives,” Wyden said. “As Congress debates solutions to protect our privacy and civil liberties, the MITRE report could provide important information about how these cameras and other surveillance programs are already impacting Americans’ rights. The White House should make MITRE’s findings public as soon as possible.”

Wyden was the first member of Congress to question Flock over its security and privacy practices, and has defended Americans’ privacy rights against unnecessary government surveillance for decades.

The full letter is available here.

###
